trial_name: TOMAHAWK — Angiography after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest without ST-Segment Elevation (2021)
citation: Desch S, Freund A, Akin I, Behnes M, Preusch MR, Zelniker TA, et al. Angiography after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest without ST-segment elevation. N Engl J Med. 2021;385:2544-2553
trial_type: RCT — investigator-initiated, prospective, randomised, multicentre, open-label, parallel-group strategy trial
one_liner: In resuscitated OHCA without ST-segment elevation, routine immediate coronary angiography did not reduce 30-day mortality compared to delayed or selective angiography and showed a signal compatible with harm.

pico.population: Adults aged ≥30 years with resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of possible coronary origin and ROSC, without ST-segment elevation or new LBBB.
pico.intervention: Immediate coronary angiography strategy with revascularisation (PCI/CABG) as indicated (protocol target coronary visualisation within 60 min).
pico.comparison: Initial intensive care assessment with delayed (≥24 hours) or selective angiography strategy.

background.existing_knowledge: Acute coronary occlusion can precipitate out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet post-ROSC ECG frequently lacks ST-segment elevation. Observational registries (including PROCAT II) suggested associations between early angiography/PCI and improved outcomes, but were vulnerable to confounding by indication and immortal-time bias.
background.knowledge_gap: The COACT trial showed no survival advantage for immediate angiography in comatose OHCA with shockable rhythms without ST-elevation, leaving uncertainty for broader cohorts including nonshockable rhythms and heterogeneous causes.
background.hypothesis: A strategy of immediate coronary angiography would reduce 30-day all-cause mortality versus initial intensive care assessment with delayed or selective angiography among resuscitated OHCA patients without ST-segment elevation.

methods.design: Investigator-initiated, prospective, randomised, multicentre, open-label, parallel-group strategy trial.
methods.setting: 31 enrolling sites across Germany and Denmark (cardiac ICU and general medical ICU settings).

inclusion: Documented resuscitated OHCA of possible coronary origin
No ST-segment elevation on post-resuscitation ECG
exclusion: ST-segment elevation or new left bundle branch block (LBBB)
Obvious extracardiac cause (trauma, severe intracranial hemorrhage, intoxication, drowning)
Persistent hemodynamic or electrical instability requiring immediate angiography (cardiogenic shock or life-threatening arrhythmias felt due to acute ischemia)
Enrolment in another interfering interventional trial

methods.intervention: Immediate coronary angiography with revascularisation (PCI/CABG) as indicated by findings; protocol target coronary visualisation within 60 minutes of presentation.
methods.comparison: Initial intensive care assessment with delayed or selective angiography after ≥24 hours, or earlier if urgent criteria emerged (cardiogenic shock, refractory electrical instability, evolving ischemia, or new ST-elevation).
methods.blinding: Open-label treatment assignment; non-mortality outcomes adjudicated by a clinical events committee.
methods.sample_size_power: 558 patients planned to detect an HR of 0.674 (30-day mortality 46% to 34%) with 90% power at 5% significance level; group-sequential design with one interim analysis after 109 deaths.
secondary_outcomes: Composite of death or severe neurologic deficit (CPC 3–5) at 30 days
Severe neurologic deficit at 30 days among survivors with available CPC
Acute renal failure requiring renal-replacement therapy
methods.follow_up: 30 days for primary endpoint (protocol planned additional follow-up to 12 months).

headline_bullets: 554 participants randomised (530 analysed in primary mITT population: 265 immediate vs 265 delayed/selective).
Routine immediate angiography did not reduce 30-day all-cause mortality (54.0% vs 46.0%; HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.00–1.63, p=0.06).
Composite of death or severe neurologic deficit occurred more frequently with immediate angiography (64.3% vs 55.6%; RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.00–1.34).
Immediate angiography was associated with a statistically significant delay in initiating targeted temperature management (median 153 min vs 119 min).

outcomes_table.note: Primary analysis mITT population; excluded 20 consent withdrawals requiring deletion and 4 protocol violations.

outcomes_table.outcome: Composite: death or severe neurologic deficit at 30 days
outcomes_table.note: Severe neurologic deficit defined as CPC 3–5; denominators reflect available neurological status data.

outcomes_table.outcome: Severe neurologic deficit at 30 days (among survivors)
outcomes_table.note: Evaluated among survivors with available CPC assessment.

outcomes_table.outcome: Acute renal failure requiring renal-replacement therapy

outcomes_table.note: Hodges–Lehmann estimate for between-group difference in medians.

safety: Moderate or severe bleeding (BARC 2–5): 4.6% (12/260) in immediate vs 3.4% (8/232) in delayed/selective (RR 1.34; 95% CI 0.57–3.14).
Stroke at 30 days: 1.6% (4/258) in immediate vs 2.1% (5/242) in delayed/selective (RR 1.13; 95% CI 0.33–3.84).
Acute renal failure requiring renal-replacement therapy: 18.9% (49/259) in immediate vs 15.8% (38/241) in delayed/selective (RR 1.14; 95% CI 0.78–1.68).

domains.notes: Central, web-based block randomisation with changing block sizes, stratified by site. Allocation concealment maintained.
Open-label design; co-interventions and care limitations could be influenced. Mortality objective; other events adjudicated blinded.

554 randomised; 530 in mITT primary analysis. 24 excluded: 20 consent withdrawals requiring full data deletion (14 immediate vs 6 delayed) and 4 eligibility violations (2 in-hospital arrest, 2 STEMI).

Angiography performed in 95.5% vs 62.2% (RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.41–1.67). Median time to angiography 2.9 h (IQR 2.2–3.9) vs 46.9 h (IQR 26.1–116.6). PCI performed in 22.6% vs 18.9% (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.86–1.67). Thrombectomy in 8.3% vs 3.8% (RR 2.20, 95% CI 1.06–4.57). TTM used in 78.9% vs 82.3% (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88–1.05); time to TTM initiation median 153 min vs 119 min (HLE diff 33 min, 95% CI 21–50). Safety crossover: 7 immediate to delayed, 22 delayed to immediate.

Median age 69 vs 71; female 30.2% vs 29.1%. Initial shockable rhythm 53.3% vs 58.7%; collapse-to-ROSC 15 vs 15 min; lactate 4.6 vs 4.4 mmol/L; pH 7.26 vs 7.28. Modest prognostic imbalance in shockable rhythm favoring control arm.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong given central randomisation and objective primary endpoint, limited by open-label design and post-randomisation exclusions.

domains.notes: Includes both shockable (53–59%) and nonshockable rhythms. Excludes STEMI, new LBBB, and hemodynamically/electrically unstable patients.
Conducted in European tertiary centers with 24/7 cath labs and ICU post-ROSC pathways. Results apply directly to clinically stable non-STEMI post-ROSC patients.

external_validity.verdict: Good generalisability for comatose post-ROSC OHCA patients without ST-elevation in tertiary centers, but inapplicable to unstable patients requiring emergent revascularisation.

strengths: Clinically important, pragmatic strategy question in a high-stakes OHCA cohort.
Multicentre design including both shockable and nonshockable initial rhythms.
Meaningful separation in angiography timing (median 2.9 h vs 46.9 h) with high procedural adherence.
Pre-specified statistical design with interim analysis and robust sensitivity analyses.
limitations: Open-label design created potential for performance bias in post-ROSC co-interventions.
Modified ITT population due to post-randomisation consent withdrawals demanding full data deletion.
High angiography rate in delayed arm (62.2%) tested routine immediate vs selective strategy rather than PCI vs medical therapy.
Power calculation assumed a large 12% absolute mortality reduction (46% to 34%).
Excluded patients with cardiogenic shock or refractory electrical instability.

critical_appraisal.summary: High-quality pragmatic trial demonstrating that routine immediate angiography after non-STEMI OHCA provides no mortality benefit and may delay critical ICU interventions like targeted temperature management.
strengths: Clear strategy separation with multi-country ICU representation.
weaknesses: Open-label administration leading to modest delays in post-ROSC bundle care in immediate group.
Post-randomisation exclusions from mandatory consent-withdrawal data deletions.

sections.authors_conclusion: Among resuscitated OHCA patients without ST-segment elevation, an immediate coronary angiography strategy did not provide a 30-day mortality benefit over delayed or selective angiography.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not routinely send stable post-ROSC OHCA patients without ST-elevation immediately to the cath lab; prioritize ICU stabilization and temperature management, reserving angiography for delayed or selective indication.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Comatose post-ROSC OHCA patients without ST-segment elevation or ongoing hemodynamic/electrical instability.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean angiography is withheld entirely; 62.2% in the delayed group received cath based on clinical selection.
implementation_caveats: Immediate cath lab activation can delay core post-resuscitation bundles including targeted temperature management (median 33 min delay in trial).
Maintain rapid cath lab capability if patients develop cardiogenic shock, electrical storm, or secondary STEMI.

controversies.notes: Primary outcome HR 1.28 (p=0.06) and composite endpoint RR 1.16 (95% CI 1.00–1.34) suggest potential harm from routine immediate cath, likely mediated by delays in critical ICU bundles.
62.2% of delayed group received cath (median 46.9 h), confirming this was a strategy comparison (immediate vs triage-driven) rather than invasive vs conservative management.

context_related_trials.relation: Found no survival benefit for immediate vs delayed angiography in comatose non-STEMI OHCA with shockable rhythms.
Observational registry suggesting benefit from early PCI, likely confounded by selection and immortal-time bias.
Pilot RCT in non-STEMI OHCA showing no benefit for immediate angiography, aligning with TOMAHAWK results.
Pilot RCT in non-STEMI OHCA underpowered but directionally aligned with neutral/harm findings for routine early cath.

unresolved_questions: Optimal timing window for delayed angiography in clinically stable non-STEMI post-ROSC patients.
Precision biomarker or imaging tools to identify non-STEMI post-ROSC subgroups with hidden acute coronary occlusions.

numbers_to_remember: Angiography timing: 2.9 h vs 46.9 h; TTM delay: 153 min vs 119 min
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In post-ROSC OHCA without ST-elevation, prioritize ICU stabilization and TTM over routine immediate transfer to the cath lab.
